description: BOT Battalion is a multidisciplinary team of developers, AI/ML enthusiasts, and problem-solvers passionate about transforming complex data into practical solutions for real-world challenges.
summary:
We developed FireSync, an interactive platform for exploring NASA FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS hotspot observations, with sensor harmonization at its core. MODIS and VIIRS observe activity at different spatial resolutions and acquisition times, making their raw counts difficult to compare directly. FireSync places observations on common spatial and temporal grids, provides paired-sensor diagnostics and displays supported historical Aqua-equivalent estimates while preserving the original sensor records. Derived indicators and estimates are clearly labelled as exploratory.

The platform combines interactive maps, daily and monthly calendars, historical comparisons, regional monitoring and downloadable data. An optional AI Investigator uses application data tools to explain sensor differences, detection evidence and analytical findings.

FireSync helps researchers, students, regional teams and communities understand satellite observed activity more clearly. By exposing sources, missing observations, model support and uncertainty, it makes harmonization transparent and supports informed analysis without presenting hotspots as confirmed wildfires or historical patterns as future predictions.
details:
FireSync is an interactive platform developed by BOT Battalion to explore and compare NASA FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS hotspot observations. It addresses the challenge of harmonizing observations from sensors with different spatial resolutions, acquisition times and detection characteristics. Our approach preserves the original sensor records, explains their differences and presents derived comparisons with their methods and limitations visible.

Users begin by selecting a region, searching for a place or drawing an area on an interactive map. They can toggle MODIS and VIIRS layers, inspect individual observations and explore acquisition time, satellite platform, confidence and fire radiative power (FRP). Charts support sensor-separated count and FRP comparisons, while geographic tools provide detection density, candidate hotspot clusters, coverage summaries and supported comparisons between regions or periods. Regional CSV downloads retain relevant source and filter information.

FireSync keeps live monitoring and historical analysis distinct. Live observations come from the NASA FIRMS near-real-time Area API within a rolling one to five UTC day window. A separate local historical archive supports observation queries, yearly summaries and a global daily calendar. Monthly AgniCalendar provides regional analysis using a separate 10 km Equal Earth grid. This separation preserves the actual resolution and population of each product: monthly aggregates are never converted into invented daily or weekly observations.

The monthly calendar helps users explore recurring seasonal activity and compare a selected month with eligible historical years. It displays the historical median, empirical percentile, baseline years and valid-year count. Comparisons require at least five other eligible years with matching product-population characteristics. Selected activity at or above the 95th percentile is labelled unusually high; insufficient history remains explicitly unavailable. Historical peak months describe past observed patterns, not future fire predictions.

Our sensor-comparison tools include nominal footprint diagrams, point and footprint matching, and paired observation diagnostics. The live analysis framework also provides an explicitly exploratory activity index on common cell-day support. Separately, AgniCalendar displays precomputed Random Forest Aqua-equivalent estimates for supported historical MODIS Aqua and VIIRS Suomi-NPP populations. These estimates remain distinct from original counts and are restricted to approved model support. They are not presented as a complete corrected VIIRS series or a universally validated fire-count model.

Early monitoring makes regional observation tracking accessible without requiring coordinates. Users can search for a place, tap the inline map or select a rectangle, then configure sensor-specific count and optional FRP thresholds. The server checks the selected live window and records in-app alerts when the condition is satisfied and previously unseen eligible observations are present. An initial check can include existing acquisitions. Monitoring operates while the server runs; acquisition time is not ignition time.

FireSync also includes an optional AI Investigator powered by Groq. Users can ask natural-language questions about observations, historical activity, sensor differences and selected detections. The assistant uses deterministic application tools to retrieve analytical results, then explains them in accessible language. It supports detection evidence cards, candidate-cluster investigations, sensor explanations and report generation. Supported map actions pass through validated application controls. Core maps, calendars and monitoring work independently of AI explanations, and provider credentials remain on the server.

We developed FireSync using React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, MapLibre GL JS and Motion for the interface, with Node.js and Express for APIs, analysis and monitoring. Python supports data preparation and validation, while DuckDB and Parquet support historical queries. Optional JSON stores preserve ingestion records, watches and alerts. The application runs on a standard computer through a modern browser with suitable graphics support; online features require network access, and historical views require the separately supplied datasets.

The project’s creativity lies in connecting scientific comparison, visual exploration and natural-language explanation within one workflow. Our team considered accessibility, sensor identity, geographic scope, processing versions, missing data, source attribution and uncertainty throughout development.

The intended impact is to help researchers, students, regional teams and communities understand satellite-observed activity more clearly. FireSync supports transparent exploration and reproducible analysis while consistently distinguishing thermal anomalies from confirmed wildfires, burned area and forecasts.
